title: How a US Startup Can Hire Engineers in India, No Entity
summary: Yes, a US startup can hire engineers in India without an entity, via a global contractor or an employer of record. Here is when each fits, what it costs, and how to switch.
body_markdown:
Yes, a US startup can hire engineers in India without an entity, and there are two legal ways to do it: pay them as global contractors, or put them on payroll through an employer of record (EOR). The right one depends on how the engineer actually works for you, not on what the contract says.


This guide is for founders at US-headquartered startups under 50 people who found a great developer in Bengaluru, Pune or Hyderabad and have no Indian legal entity. It covers when each route fits, where misclassification bites, what an EOR handles (payroll, PF, gratuity, contracts), what you should budget, and how to move later. If you already have your own Indian entity, you need a different setup, and the last section says why.


## Can a US company hire an employee in India without an entity?


Yes, but you cannot employ someone directly in India without a local legal entity, so the workaround is to have someone else be the legal employer. That someone is an employer of record. The alternative is to skip employment entirely and engage the engineer as an independent contractor.


Two facts frame the decision. First, Indian employment carries statutory obligations: employer contributions to the Employees' Provident Fund (EPF), gratuity liability, payroll tax withholding and written employment terms. Second, those obligations attach to the working relationship, not the label on your agreement. A full-time engineer who works your hours, takes direction from your CTO and works for nobody else looks like an employee to a regulator, whatever the paperwork says.


So the question is never just "can we hire in India without an entity." It is "which structure matches how this person really works."


## Two legal routes: global contractor or employer of record


The two routes are a global contractor agreement or an employer of record, and they solve different problems.


An employer of record is an organization that becomes the legal employer of your worker in their country. The EOR signs the employment contract, runs payroll, withholds taxes, makes statutory contributions and handles local compliance, while you direct the day-to-day work. A contractor arrangement is not employment at all. The engineer invoices you, pays their own taxes and runs their own business. A related acronym, PEO, covers co-employment inside one country (typically the US) and does not let you employ people in a country where you have no entity, so it is the wrong tool for this job.


Here is the practical split:


Global contractor Employer of record


Legal relationship Independent business serving you Employee of the EOR, working for you


Who pays statutory costs The contractor The EOR, billed to you


Fit Defined projects, multiple clients Full-time, ongoing, managed roles


Main risk Misclassification Higher monthly cost

### What is an employer of record service?


An employer of record (EOR) is a company that legally employs your worker in their country on your behalf. For a US startup hiring an engineer in India, the EOR holds the Indian entity, signs the employment contract, runs payroll and statutory contributions, and files the required paperwork. You still direct the daily work, set priorities and own the output. You pay the EOR a fee, and you never need to set up your own Indian company.


### Employer of record vs PEO: which fits a US startup hiring in India?


A PEO co-employs people inside a country where your company already has a legal entity, so it does not solve the India problem for a US startup with no Indian entity. An EOR is the legal employer in the foreign country, which is the benefit here: compliant hiring without incorporating. The costs are ongoing fees and less direct control over HR terms. A PEO adds nothing for a worker based in India.


## When a contractor is fine, and when it becomes misclassification


A contractor is fine when the engineer is genuinely independent: scoped deliverables, their own tools and schedule, other clients, and no day-to-day management from you.


It becomes misclassification when the relationship behaves like a job. Watch for these signals:


-


The engineer works full-time or exclusively for you


-


You set their hours or require them in your standups and sprint cycles


-


They report to a manager on your team and are listed on your org chart


-


The engagement is open-ended rather than tied to a project


If several of those are true, assume a regulator could treat the person as an employee regardless of the contract. The exposure is retrospective: back contributions to provident fund, gratuity, tax and related liabilities that nobody budgeted for. A startup that finds this out during due diligence on a Series A has a much worse week than one that chose an EOR on day one.


The rule of thumb: contractors for projects, an EOR for a teammate. If you picture this engineer on your team page in a year, put them on an EOR.


## What an EOR handles for Indian engineers: payroll, PF, gratuity, contracts, compliance


An EOR takes over the employer side of Indian employment so you do not have to learn it. For an engineer in India that means five things.


**Contracts.** A compliant Indian employment agreement, with local terms for notice, leave and termination, plus onboarding.


**Payroll.** Monthly salary run through Indian payroll, with income tax withheld and remitted.


**Provident fund.** Employer EPF contributions, roughly 12% of basic wages, subject to the wage base and employee eligibility (confirm current rules for each hire).


**Gratuity.** A liability that accrues at about 4.81% of eligible wages and is payable after five years of continuous service in the usual case.


**Compliance.** Statutory registrations, filings and record-keeping that the legal employer owes.


One limit to be straight about: an EOR does not automatically erase permanent establishment (PE) risk. That depends on what your engineers do and on the US-India tax treaty, especially whether anyone habitually negotiates or concludes contracts for your company in India. Ordinary engineering work is generally lower risk, but get tax advice for your facts.


### What does an employer of record do day to day?


An employer of record handles the legal employer duties so you do not need an entity. That means issuing a compliant Indian employment contract, running monthly payroll, deducting and paying tax and provident fund, accruing gratuity, and keeping statutory records. It also manages onboarding and offboarding paperwork. You manage the engineer's work, goals and performance, while the EOR carries the employer compliance.


## What it costs: salary, employer contributions and EOR fees


Budget for three layers: the engineer's salary, employer statutory costs, and the EOR's fee.


Salary is whatever you and the engineer agree. Employer costs sit on top: about 12% of basic wages for EPF plus a gratuity accrual of about 4.81% of eligible wages, with exact figures depending on wage structure and eligibility. The EOR fee is the third layer, and providers price it differently. EOR starting prices vary across vendors, typically charged either as a monthly fee per employee or as a percentage of monthly processed payroll. Treat those as ranges to compare against, not quotes.


When you request quotes, ask each provider the same four questions:


1.


Is the fee flat per employee or a percentage of payroll?


2.


Are PF and gratuity passed through at cost or marked up?


3.


What do onboarding and offboarding cost?


4.


Is there a minimum term or a fee to convert the hire later?


Contractors skip the employer-contribution layer entirely. That is why they look cheaper, and why misclassifying a full-time engineer as one is a false economy.


### How do you compare employer of record providers on price?


Compare EOR providers on total monthly cost per employee, not the headline fee. Total cost is the engineer's salary, employer statutory contributions, the EOR's fee, and any extras such as onboarding, equipment, benefits or termination charges. Request a written quote for the same salary from each provider, and ask what happens to pricing if you add more hires or later move the person to your own entity.

## How to move from contractor to EOR, or to your own entity later


Switching is easier than founders fear, as long as you plan it before the relationship has hardened into a job.


**Contractor to EOR.** End the contractor agreement, sign an employment contract through the EOR, and set a clean start date so there is no overlap. Agree the new salary structure up front, because employment adds statutory components a flat contractor rate did not have. Do this as soon as the engineer becomes full-time and open-ended.


**EOR to your own entity.** Once you have enough people in India to justify the overhead, you can incorporate and transfer employees from the EOR to your entity. Ask your EOR about transfer terms and notice periods at signing.


If you have an Indian subsidiary, you need a different setup than the one described here.


## FAQ: IP ownership, permanent establishment risk, and when you need your own entity


These are the questions founders ask most once they have picked a route. The short version: get the IP clause in writing, treat PE risk as fact-specific, and move to your own entity when headcount makes it cheaper than the EOR.


## How do you choose an employer of record provider in 2026?


Choose an EOR by checking what it handles for your specific country, not by a ranked list. For India, ask whether it covers payroll, provident fund, gratuity and compliant contracts for engineers, how its fees are structured, and how it handles IP assignment. Also check whether it supports global contractors, so you can switch later without changing vendor. ## What should you look for in employer of record reviews?


Read EOR reviews for evidence about the things that go wrong: slow onboarding, payroll errors, unclear fees and weak support when an employee has a problem. Favour reviews from companies of your size hiring in the same country, since a review from a 500-person firm hiring in Europe says little about a 15-person US startup hiring in India. Ask each provider for references, and confirm in writing what the monthly fee includes and what is billed separately.


## Start with an EOR for teammates and contractors for projects


If the engineer will be a full-time part of your team, put them on an employer of record from day one. If they are scoped, independent and serving other clients, a global contractor agreement is fine. That single test prevents most of the misclassification risk founders worry about.
